subject: Agriculture
title: What Is an Aquifer
description: Learn What Is an Aquifer in one minute.

hook.text: Beneath your feet, vast layers of rock and gravel hold water like underground sponges. These are aquifers.

buildup.text: Water seeps into the ground through rain, filling porous rock layers over thousands of years.

discovery.text: Wells tap aquifers by drilling into water-saturated rock. A pump brings the water to the surface.

twist.text: Some aquifers recharge quickly from rainfall. Others, like the Ogallala, hold ancient water that barely refills.

climax.text: Globally, 70% of groundwater withdrawals go to agriculture. Farms depend on water banked underground.

punchline.text: Aquifers are savings accounts. Some refill. Many don't.

quiz.question: What percentage of global groundwater withdrawals goes to agriculture?

details.summary: An aquifer is an underground layer of water-bearing rock or sediment that stores and transmits groundwater. This topic introduces aquifer types, how they recharge, and why understanding aquifers is fundamental to managing agricultural water supplies sustainably.
details.whyItMatters: Aquifers supply about 40% of global irrigation water. Yet they are invisible and often poorly understood, leading to over-extraction that threatens future food production in many regions.
takeaways: Aquifers are made of permeable rock or sediment like sand, gravel, and limestone
Confined aquifers are trapped between impermeable layers and recharge very slowly
Unconfined aquifers recharge from surface water but are vulnerable to contamination

faq.question: What is an aquifer and how does it store water?
faq.answer: An aquifer is a geological formation of permeable rock, sand, or gravel that holds water in pore spaces and fractures. Water fills the gaps between particles, and the formation transmits water slowly, functioning like a vast underground sponge.

faq.question: What is the difference between confined and unconfined aquifers?
faq.answer: Unconfined aquifers have a water table open to surface recharge from rain and rivers. Confined aquifers are sandwiched between impermeable clay layers, are under pressure, and recharge extremely slowly from distant locations.
